a: In the days of Ahaz son of Jotham
p: Damascus and Samaria tried to force Judah into a revolt against Assyria. This chapter is Isaiah's side of that crisis.
b: Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria (744–727 BC) was conquering the west. Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Israel formed a coalition to resist him and wanted Judah in it. When Ahaz refused, they marched on Jerusalem to replace him (7:6). Scholars call this the Syro-Ephraimite war (734–732 BC). 2 Kings tells it in almost the same words: "That was when Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to Jerusalem for battle" (2 Kings 16:5). Kings adds what Isaiah only implies: Ahaz sent silver and gold to Assyria and called himself its servant (2 Kings 16:7–8). 2 Chronicles 28:5–8 reports heavy losses for Judah. The verse summarizes the whole war before telling how it began.

a: But he was not able to win the fight against it.
p: The Hebrew says "he was not able", singular; the Great Isaiah Scroll and 2 Kings 16:5 say "they".
b: The Masoretic Text has yakhol, "he was able", which may mean Rezin as the leader of the attack. The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) has the plural yakhlu, "they were able", as 2 Kings 16:5 does, and so does the Greek. The meaning hardly changes. The Plain keeps the Hebrew "he".
orig: ולא יכל (velo' yakhol), 'and he was not able'

a: Aram has settled in Ephraim
p: The verb means "come to rest": Aram's troops are camped in Ephraim, or Aram has leaned on Ephraim as an ally.
b: Nachah 'al is used of locusts settling on a land (Exodus 10:14) and of the Spirit resting on someone (11:2, the same verb). Here it may mean Aram's army has arrived and camped in Ephraim's territory, close to Judah, or that Aram has joined forces with Ephraim. The Greek has "Aram has agreed with Ephraim". Either way the news means war is near. "Ephraim" is Isaiah's name for the northern kingdom of Israel, after its largest tribe.
orig: נחה ארם על אפרים (nachah Aram 'al Efrayim)

a: The house of David
t: Why "house of David" and a plural "you"
p: Isaiah addresses the whole royal dynasty, the line God had promised to keep (2 Samuel 7:16).
b: The message is to Ahaz, but it is framed as news to "the house of David", and in 7:9, 7:13 and 7:14 the Hebrew "you" is plural. The issue is the dynasty itself. The coalition wanted to end David's line in Jerusalem by setting up a king of its own (7:6). God had promised David, "Your house and your kingdom will be made secure forever in front of you" (2 Samuel 7:16). The chapter asks whether the house of David will rely on that promise. The same Hebrew root, aman, "be firm, made secure", is used in 2 Samuel 7:16 and in Isaiah's warning in 7:9.
orig: בית דוד (bet David); plural לכם (lakhem), 'to you all' (7:14)

a: Shear-jashub
p: The name of Isaiah's son is a message: it can be heard as a threat or as a promise.
b: She'ar yashuv means "a remnant will return". It can sound like a warning (only a remnant will be left) or a hope (a remnant will come back, to the land or to God; shuv means both "return" and "repent"). 10:20–22 plays on it both ways. Isaiah takes the boy to the king without explanation: his name is part of the message. He is the first of the children who are "signs and omens in Israel" (8:18), with Maher-shalal-hash-baz (8:1–4) and perhaps Immanuel (7:14).

a: the water channel of the Upper Pool, on the main road to the Launderers' Field
t: The same spot, a generation later
p: Ahaz was probably inspecting Jerusalem's water supply before a siege. Assyria's envoy will stand in the same place.
b: A city under siege lives or dies by its water, so the king was likely checking the channel that fed a pool from the Gihon spring. Launderers needed plenty of water to wash and bleach cloth, so their field lay near it, outside the walls. The site is not certainly known. About thirty years later, the Assyrian officers "came to Jerusalem" and "took their stand by the water channel of the Upper Pool, on the main road to the Launderers' Field" (2 Kings 18:17; Isaiah 36:2). The book means readers to set the two scenes side by side: Ahaz refused to trust God there, and his son Hezekiah was tested there.

a: two tail ends of smoking logs
p: The two kings look like a raging fire, but they are logs almost burned out: all smoke and little flame.
b: A zanav is a "tail", here the charred end of a firebrand. The kings' anger is hot ("the hot anger of Rezin"), but they themselves are nearly spent. Within about two years both were dead: Tiglath-pileser took Damascus and killed Rezin (2 Kings 16:9, 732 BC), and Pekah was assassinated by Hoshea (2 Kings 15:30). Isaiah tells the king to keep calm because the threat is smaller than it looks.
orig: שני זנבות האודים העשנים (shene zanvot ha'udim ha'ashenim)

a: Remaliah's son
p: In the speeches Isaiah never names Pekah: to call a man only "son of" his father was a put-down.
b: Rezin is named, but in the speeches Pekah is always "Remaliah's son" (7:4, 5, 9; 8:6); only the narrator gives his name (7:1). Saul did the same to David, calling him "the son of Jesse" (1 Samuel 20:27, 31), and so did Nabal (1 Samuel 25:10). The phrase may also hint that Pekah was a usurper with no royal father: he had seized the throne by murder (2 Kings 15:25).

a: the son of Tabeal
p: The name is probably Tabeel, "God is good"; the Hebrew vowels make it Tabeal, "good-for-nothing".
b: The consonants spell an Aramaic name, Tav'el, "God is good". The vowels the Masoretes added make it Tav'al, which sounds like "no good", probably a scribal joke at the puppet king's expense; the Plain follows those vowels. Who he was is unknown. Some think he was a Judean prince from a branch of the royal family, others an Aramean or a Tyrian noble. W. F. Albright linked him to a "land of Tabeel" east of the Jordan named in an Assyrian letter from Nimrud. Either way, the coalition meant to end David's line on the throne.

a: The Lord GOD says this
p: A messenger opened with "So says the king". The prophets open the same way: the words that follow are the LORD's.
b: Koh amar, "so says", is how a royal messenger delivered his master's words (2 Kings 18:19, "The great king, the king of Assyria, says this"). Prophets use it to show that they speak for the LORD, not for themselves. "The Lord GOD" renders Adonai YHWH: Adonai means "Lord", and YHWH, God's personal name, is printed "GOD" in capitals when it follows Adonai, so that the English does not read "Lord LORD".
orig: כה אמר אדני יהוה (koh amar Adonai YHWH)

a: In sixty-five more years
p: Israel fell in 722 BC, only about twelve years later. The sixty-five years are a puzzle.
b: If the words were spoken in 734 BC, sixty-five years point to about 669 BC. Many conservative interpreters note that Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal settled foreigners in Samaria around then (Ezra 4:2, 10), which ended Ephraim as "a people": the fall of 722 was the beginning, the resettlement the end. Many critical scholars think the line is a later note added to the oracle, because it breaks the pattern of 7:8a and 7:9a; some move it to after 7:9a. Others think the number counts from an earlier prophecy (Amos 7:11). The point of the verse stands either way: Ephraim has no future.

a: If you will not hold firm, you will not be held firm.
p: Two forms of one Hebrew verb: "believe" and "be made secure". The Plain matches 2 Chronicles 20:20.
b: Im lo ta'aminu ki lo te'amenu. The root aman means "be firm, be reliable". The first verb (Hiphil) means "trust, believe", literally "stand firm on"; the second (Niphal) means "be made firm, be secure", the word for David's house in 2 Samuel 7:16. Jehoshaphat uses the same pair: "Hold firm to the LORD your God, and you will be held firm" (2 Chronicles 20:20), and the Plain renders both alike. The "you" is plural, the whole house of David. The Greek has "if you do not believe, neither will you understand", and from its Latin form Augustine drew his motto, "Unless you believe, you will not understand." The Great Isaiah Scroll spells the second verb like the first.
orig: אם לא תאמינו כי לא תאמנו (im lo ta'aminu ki lo te'amenu)

a: down in Sheol
p: The same consonants can be read "to Sheol" or "ask it". The Masoretic vowels give "ask".
b: The Hebrew consonants sh'lh can be read she'olah, "to Sheol, downward", or she'alah, "ask!", as the Masoretes vowel it ("go deep, ask!"). Most modern versions read "Sheol", which matches "high, up above" in the next line, and the Plain does too, as does Jerome's Latin, in profundum inferni, "into the depth of the underworld". The Greek has only "into the depth" (eis bathos). The offer is huge: any sign, from the depths of the world of the dead to the sky. Sheol is the Hebrew name for the place of the dead.

a: I won't test the LORD
p: Ahaz quotes the law, but the reader knows he had already decided to trust Assyria instead.
b: "Do not put the LORD your God to the test" (Deuteronomy 6:16) forbids demanding proof from God out of doubt. But here God himself offers the sign, so refusing it is not humility. Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, read Ahaz's answer as a mask: he would not ask because he did not want to be bound to trust God. 2 Kings 16:7–8 shows what he did instead. Hezekiah, his son, will accept a sign (38:7–8), and Gideon asked for two (Judges 6:36–40).

a: my God
p: In 7:11 the LORD is "your God" to Ahaz. After his refusal Isaiah says "my God".
b: The shift is small and sharp. Ahaz was offered a sign from "the LORD your God" (7:11). Having turned it down, he hears Isaiah speak of "my God", as if the king had stepped outside the relationship. "Wearing out" people and God means testing their patience with stubborn unbelief (1:14; 43:24).

a: the young woman
p: The most debated word in Isaiah. 'Almah means a young woman; the Greek parthenos, quoted by Matthew, usually means virgin.
b: 'Almah is a young woman of marriageable age. It is used of Rebekah at the well (Genesis 24:43), of Moses' sister (Exodus 2:8), of the girls with tambourines in a festal procession (Psalm 68:25) and of "a man with a young woman" (Proverbs 30:19). Hebrew has another word, betulah, often translated "virgin"; how much either word says about virginity is the heart of the debate (see the next note). The Greek translators chose parthenos, which Matthew 1:23 quotes. Modern translations divide. The NIV, ESV, NASB, CSB, NKJV and NLT put "virgin" in the text, the NIV and ESV with "young woman" in a footnote; the RSV, NRSV, NABRE, NJPS, REB, CEB and NET put "young woman" in the text. The article, "the young woman", points to someone Isaiah and Ahaz knew or could see. See the variant on this word and the chapter page.
orig: העלמה (ha'almah), 'the young woman'; Greek ἡ παρθένος (hē parthenos)

a: the young woman
p: Each side has standard arguments from the Hebrew words, the Greek and the context. Both read the evidence in good faith.
b: For "virgin". Betulah is not a technical word for a virgin either: Joel 1:8 uses it of a woman mourning "the husband of her youth", and Genesis 24:16 must add that no man had been with Rebekah, so 'almah need be no weaker (Wenham). Rebekah is called a betulah (Genesis 24:16) and then an 'almah (Genesis 24:43). No text uses 'almah of a married woman, and Song of Songs 6:8 sets the 'alamot apart from queens and concubines. Jewish translators chose parthenos two centuries before Jesus, and a sign that could reach "down in Sheol" (7:11) suggests more than an ordinary birth. For "young woman". 'Almah marks age, not virginity. Harah is a present adjective, "is pregnant", which suits a woman who has already conceived (see the next note). The Greek uses parthenos even of Dinah after she was raped (Genesis 34:3). Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion all put neanis, "young woman". The cognate Ugaritic word glmt appears in a wedding poem announcing that a bride will bear a son. And the sign is tied to a few years in Ahaz's time (7:16).
r: Joel 1:8; Genesis 24:16; Genesis 24:43; Song of Songs 6:8; Genesis 34:3; 7:16

a: is pregnant and about to have a son
p: Hara is an adjective, "pregnant", with no tense: the Hebrew can mean she already is, or she will be.
b: Hebrew harah is an adjective ("pregnant"), followed by a participle or verb, "and bearing". Hebrew sentences without a verb take their time from the context. The same words are said to Hagar, "Look, you are with child, and you will bear a son" (Genesis 16:11), when she is already pregnant, and to Samson's mother, "You are going to be pregnant and have a son" (Judges 13:5), before she is. The Plain says "is pregnant", the more natural sense of the adjective, as many modern versions do (NRSV, NJPS, NABRE, CEB). The KJV, NIV, ESV and others have a future; so do Swete's Greek, "will conceive" (lēmpsetai), and Matthew 1:23, "will be pregnant" (en gastri hexei). The wording follows a common birth announcement, which in each case ends with the child's name.

a: Immanuel
p: The child has been identified as Hezekiah, Isaiah's son, any child born that year, a future king, or Jesus.
b: The name means "God is with us" ('immanu El). The main readings: Hezekiah, Ahaz's son and heir, the view Justin Martyr's Jewish partner Trypho gives (Dialogue 67), though by 2 Kings 16:2 and 18:2 he was already born; Isaiah's own son, with the prophetess as the young woman (Rashi, Ibn Ezra), since 8:3–4 repeats the time-sign; any child born in Judah that year, a mother naming her baby in hope; a royal child of the future, since Immanuel's land is Judah (8:8) and the child-king of 9:6–7 and 11:1–5 seems to be the same figure; Jesus, directly, as Calvin and Edward J. Young read it, since no birth in Ahaz's day is recorded as a sign; or first a child of that time and finally Jesus, a double or typological fulfillment, as many Christian scholars hold. Matthew 1:23 applies it to Jesus. See the chapter page.
orig: עמנו אל ('immanu El), 'with us is God'

a: Curds and honey
t: Food of plenty, or food of a ruined land?
p: Curds and honey sound like a land of milk and honey, but 7:21–22 makes them the food of survivors when farms are gone.
b: Chem'ah is soured milk or soft cheese, like yogurt, and devash is honey, probably wild honey or date syrup. They recall "a land flowing with milk and honey" (Exodus 3:8), and some read them as royal or even heavenly food, a sign of blessing. But 7:21–25 explains them: when Assyria has wasted the farms and vineyards, the few people left will live on what herds and wild bees give. So the child grows up in a land being emptied. The food marks both judgment on Judah's farms and survival for a remnant.

a: say no to the bad and choose the good
t: An age, not a moral test
p: Knowing good from bad is a Hebrew way to say a child is old enough to tell what is good for him: a few years.
b: The phrase marks the age when a child can make choices, as with the Israelite children who "do not yet know good from bad today" (Deuteronomy 1:39), or, at the other end of life, an old man who can no longer taste food (2 Samuel 19:35). It may mean food (spitting out what tastes bad) or right and wrong. Either way, it sets a short clock: two or three years at most. 8:4 sets a similar clock for Maher-shalal-hash-baz.
orig: מאוס ברע ובחור בטוב (ma'os bara' uvachor battov)

a: the land whose two kings fill you with dread will lie abandoned
p: Within about three years Damascus fell, Rezin was killed, Pekah was murdered and much of Israel was emptied.
b: In 733–732 BC Tiglath-pileser took Galilee and Gilead from Israel and deported their people (2 Kings 15:29), then "went up to Damascus and seized it, took its people away captive to Kir, and killed Rezin" (2 Kings 16:9). Pekah was killed by Hoshea, who paid tribute to Assyria; Tiglath-pileser's annals claim the Assyrians overthrew Pekah and set Hoshea on the throne. So the time-sign was fulfilled in Ahaz's own day. Readers who hold that 7:14 speaks only of Jesus read the "boy" of 7:16 as a different child, Shear-jashub, who was standing there (7:3).

a: It will be the king of Assyria
t: The punch line, or a later note?
p: The last words name the threat outright. Many scholars think a scribe added them; others hear Isaiah's own blow.
b: The sentence runs: the LORD will bring days on you "... the king of Assyria". The grammar is loose, and the same phrase appears in 7:20 and 8:7, where some also take it as a gloss. If it is Isaiah's, it is a hammer at the end: the king Ahaz is about to hire as his savior (2 Kings 16:7) is the disaster. "Since the day Ephraim split off from Judah" means since the kingdom divided after Solomon, about 931 BC (1 Kings 12): two hundred years of history had nothing as bad.

a: the LORD will whistle and call the fly
p: As a beekeeper whistles to his bees, the LORD will call the great powers, Egypt and Assyria.
b: The same verb, sharaq, appears in 5:26, where the LORD whistles for a far nation. The fly and the bee are swarms of soldiers, from the Nile delta and from Assyria. Assyria and Egypt did clash in the land of Israel a generation later (20:1–6; 2 Kings 18:21). Isaiah's point is that the empires come at God's signal, not by their own power, the theme of 10:5–15. Ye'ore Mitsrayim are the branches of the Nile in the delta.

a: a hired razor
p: Ahaz paid Assyria to rescue him. Isaiah says the hired razor will shave Judah itself.
b: Ahaz "sent the king of Assyria a bribe" (2 Kings 16:8) to save him from Aram and Israel. The LORD, Isaiah says, will use that hired blade on Judah. Shaving was humiliation: when Hanun "shaved half the beard off each man", it was an insult that led to war (2 Samuel 10:4). Shaving a captive's head and body was also done to slaves. The "hair of the feet" is a polite way to speak of the body's private hair: "feet" is a euphemism in Hebrew (Exodus 4:25; Ruth 3:7). "Beyond the River" means beyond the Euphrates.
orig: בתער השכירה (betaʿar hassekhirah); שער הרגלים (se'ar haraglayim)

a: a thousand pieces of silver
p: A vineyard of a thousand vines worth a thousand silver pieces was the best land a farmer could have.
b: A silver piece here is a shekel, about 11 grams of silver. The Song of Songs speaks of a vineyard of Solomon whose tenants paid "a thousand pieces of silver" each for its fruit (Song of Songs 8:11). Judah's terraced hillsides were planted with vines and olives. The picture is of the most valuable farmland returning to wild scrub, where men go only to hunt (7:24). It reverses the song of the vineyard in 5:1–7, where the LORD himself planted the choicest vines.

a: a big tablet
p: Isaiah writes the name on a large surface in plain letters, like a sign anyone can read.
b: Gillayon is rare; in 3:23 a similar word means polished mirrors, so it may be a smooth tablet of wood, metal or stone. "A common pen" (literally "a man's stylus") probably means ordinary script that ordinary people could read, not a scribe's hand. The Greek has "a new large book". The words are dated and witnessed before the child is even conceived (8:2–3), so that when events come true no one can say the prophecy was made up afterward. Compare 30:8 and Habakkuk 2:2.

a: Maher-shalal-hash-baz
t: "Quick to the plunder, swift to the spoil"
p: The longest name in the Bible is four words of war: the looters are coming fast.
b: Maher shalal chash baz is two pairs of words with the same meaning: "hurry, loot; hasten, plunder". The "For" before it (le-) may mean "belonging to", like an owner's mark on a seal, or "concerning". 8:4 explains it: Assyria will strip Damascus and Samaria. Like his brother Shear-jashub, the boy carries the message in his name (8:18).
orig: מהר שלל חש בז (maher shalal chash baz)

a: Uriah the priest
t: Two witnesses close to the king
p: Uriah later built Ahaz's Damascus altar. Zechariah may have been the king's father-in-law.
b: "Uriah the priest built the altar exactly as King Ahaz had sent from Damascus" (2 Kings 16:11): this is very likely the same man, the chief priest in Ahaz's day. Hezekiah's mother was "Abi, daughter of Zechariah" (2 Kings 18:2), and some suggest this Zechariah is the same, Ahaz's father-in-law. If so, Isaiah chose witnesses from the king's own circle, men the court could not dismiss. That one of them later followed Ahaz into a foreign altar makes the choice ironic: "reliable" refers to their standing as witnesses, not their faith.

a: the prophetess
p: She is called "the prophetess", either because she was a prophet herself or because she was the prophet's wife.
b: Nevi'ah elsewhere means a woman prophet: Miriam (Exodus 15:20), Deborah (Judges 4:4), Huldah (2 Kings 22:14). So many think Isaiah's wife had a prophetic role of her own. Rashi and Ibn Ezra read it as "the prophet's wife". Some Jewish commentators identify her with the young woman of 7:14, making her son the sign; Christian readers answer that the boys bear different names and roles. "I slept with" translates "I came near to", a common polite way of speaking about sex (Genesis 20:4; Leviticus 18:14).

a: Damascus's riches and Samaria's plunder
t: The Magi and the wealth of Damascus
p: Fulfilled in 732–722 BC; early Christian writers also read it of the Magi's gifts.
b: A baby says "Father" and "Mother" at about a year, so the prophecy points to about 732 BC, when Damascus fell (2 Kings 16:9); Samaria lost territory then and fell in 722. Justin Martyr (Dialogue 77–78) and Tertullian (An Answer to the Jews 9) read the verse of Jesus: before he could speak, the Magi from the east brought him their gold and left their old religion behind (Matthew 2:11). Few modern readers follow them, but it shows how early Christians read 7–8 as one prophecy of Christ.

a: the waters of Shiloah
p: Jerusalem's small, slow water channel stands for the LORD's quiet care, against the roaring River of Assyria.
b: Shiloach, "sent", was a channel that carried water from the Gihon spring along the slope of the City of David to a pool, before Hezekiah cut his tunnel (2 Kings 20:20). It flowed gently. Isaiah sets it against the Euphrates in flood (8:7): Judah has spurned the God who cares for Zion quietly, so it will get the great River instead. Psalm 46:4 has a similar picture of God's city: "A river! Its channels gladden the city of God". The pool of Siloam in John 9:7 takes its name from this channel; John explains it as "Sent".
orig: מי השלח (me hashiloach), 'the waters of the sent one'

a: takes joy in Rezin and Remaliah's son
p: It is odd that Judah would rejoice in its attackers. The text may be damaged, or some in Judah favored them.
b: Umesos 'et Retsin reads "and rejoicing with Rezin". Perhaps a party in Jerusalem welcomed the coalition against Assyria; perhaps "this people" here means the northern kingdom, which rejoiced in its alliance. Many scholars change one letter to read umesos, "and melting (in fear) before Rezin", which fits 7:2. The Greek paraphrases: "wanting to have Rezin and Remaliah's son as king over you". The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: the River's water, strong and abundant
p: "The River" in the Bible means the Euphrates. Its flood is the Assyrian army sweeping over Judah.
b: A river in flood is a common picture of an invading army (Jeremiah 46:7–8; 47:2). The Euphrates was Assyria's river, and "the king of Assyria with all his glory" may be a scribe's explanation of the picture, or Isaiah's own. The flood reaches "up to the neck" (8:8): Judah will nearly drown but not quite. That is what happened in 701 BC, when Sennacherib took the fortified towns of Judah and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem but did not take the city (36:1; 37:33–37).

a: Its wings will stretch out
t: Wings of flood, or wings of shelter?
p: The flood's "wings" spread over the land. With the cry "Immanuel" the image may turn into protecting wings.
b: Kenafayim, "wings", can mean the edges of a flood spreading wide, or a bird of prey covering its victim. But the verse ends with "Immanuel", and 8:10 turns that name into a cry of confidence. Some readers hear a double meaning: the same wings that threaten will turn out to be God's wings over the land (Psalm 91:4; Ruth 2:12). The Greek translates the last word as a sentence, "God is with us"; the Great Isaiah Scroll and 4QIsa-e write it as one word, a name.

a: your land, Immanuel
p: Judah is called Immanuel's land. So the child of 7:14 is linked to the land and probably to its throne.
b: Only a king or the land's true owner would have the land called his. This is one reason many readers connect Immanuel with the royal child of 9:6–7 and the shoot of Jesse in 11:1. Christian interpreters see the land of Judah as the land of Christ, and Jewish interpreters as the land of the heir of David, often Hezekiah. In 8:10 "God is with us" is the same Hebrew, 'immanu El, spoken by the people.

a: Do your worst, you peoples
p: The verb ro'u can mean "do evil", "raise the war cry" or "be broken". The Greek read it as "know".
b: The consonants r'w can come from ra'a', "do harm, be evil" or "break", or from rua', "shout the battle cry". The Greek translator read a d for the similar r: de'u, "know (this)". The Plain's "do your worst" keeps the challenge to the nations: whatever they plan against Zion will be broken (17:12–14; Psalm 2:1–4).

a: for God is with us
p: The child's name becomes the people's cry: no plan against them can stand.
b: Ki 'immanu El: the Hebrew is exactly the name of 7:14. The psalms of Zion say the same thing: "The LORD of Armies is with us" (Psalm 46:7). The words "it will not stand" also recall the LORD's verdict on the coalition's plan (7:7). Hezekiah will say the same before Sennacherib, "We have the LORD our God, to help us" (2 Chronicles 32:8). Matthew's Gospel begins with Immanuel (Matthew 1:23) and ends with Jesus' promise to be with his followers (Matthew 28:20).

a: his hand gripping me hard
p: The "strong hand" is the prophet's experience of being seized by God. The vowels of "warned me" are debated.
b: "The hand of the LORD" coming on a prophet means a powerful experience of God taking hold (Ezekiel 3:14; 2 Kings 3:15; Jeremiah 15:17). "He warned me" follows the Masoretic vowels, yissereni, from yasar, "discipline, instruct". The Great Isaiah Scroll has yesirenu, from sur, "turn aside": "he turned me (or us) away from walking in the way of this people". The sense is close.

a: 'Conspiracy!'
p: Qesher means a plot or treason. Isaiah and his followers must not share the panic of a city that sees plots everywhere.
b: Qesher is the word Athaliah screams in 2 Kings 11:14, "Conspiracy!" The "you" is plural: Isaiah and his disciples (8:16). Perhaps their opposition to the king's policy was being called treason, as Amos was accused (Amos 7:10). Or the people were calling the Aram–Israel coalition a great conspiracy and panicking. Some scholars emend qesher to qadosh, "holy", to match 8:13, but no manuscript has it. 1 Peter 3:14–15 quotes the Greek of 8:12–13: "Do not fear what they fear, and do not be shaken. Instead, in your hearts treat Christ as holy, as Lord." Peter puts "Christ" where Isaiah has "the LORD of Armies".

a: a stone that people strike their foot on
p: The LORD is both shelter and stumbling block. Paul and Peter join this verse with 28:16 and apply it to Christ.
b: The same God is a holy place for those who fear him and a rock to trip over for those who do not. Romans 9:33 joins this verse to 28:16: "Look, I am setting in Zion a stone to stumble over and a rock that trips people up, and the one who trusts in him will never be put to shame"; 1 Peter 2:8 quotes it beside Psalm 118:22. Simeon's words about Jesus, "This one is set here for many in Israel to fall and to rise" (Luke 2:34), echo it too. The Greek of Isaiah turns the sense around: "you will not meet him as a stone of stumbling". The New Testament follows the Hebrew sense here, not the Greek.

a: He will become a holy place
p: Miqdash means a sanctuary, a place of refuge. Some scholars emend it to make the verse all threat.
b: A miqdash is a holy place, where a fugitive could find asylum (1 Kings 1:50). So the line first offers refuge, then warns of stumbling. Because the rest of the verse is all danger, some scholars read moqesh, "snare", or maqshir, "one who conspires" (linking 8:12). No Hebrew manuscript has these. The Greek has "he will be your sanctuary", if you trust in him. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: both houses of Israel
p: The phrase means both kingdoms, the north (Israel) and the south (Judah), as if they were still one people.
b: Only here does the Bible say "the two houses of Israel". Isaiah treats the divided kingdoms as one family facing one God. The north has stumbled into ruin; Judah, whose capital is Jerusalem, is about to. The hope of their reunion appears in 11:13.

a: Put a seal on the teaching
t: The prophet's teaching and his disciples
p: Isaiah's message is wrapped and sealed with his disciples until events prove it true. Torah here means teaching.
b: Torah, usually "law" on this site, has its older sense here, "teaching, instruction", the prophet's own message (as in 1:10; 30:9). Te'udah, "witness", is the attested record. Legal documents were rolled, tied and sealed in front of witnesses (Jeremiah 32:10–14). The "disciples" (limmudim, "those taught") are Isaiah's circle. Many scholars see here the start of the book itself: the words were kept by a group of followers, and chapters 6:1–9:7, told partly in Isaiah's own voice, may be the record they kept. Daniel 12:4 uses the same idea of sealing.
orig: צור תעודה חתום תורה בלמדי (tsor te'udah chatom torah belimmuday)

a: I will keep looking to him
p: Hebrews puts Isaiah's words of trust, and his words about "the children", in the mouth of Jesus.
b: The Greek of 8:17 ends "and I will put my trust in him". Hebrews 2:13 quotes it, and then 8:18: "And again: 'I will put my trust in him.' And again: 'Here I am, with the children God has given me.'" For the writer of Hebrews, Jesus shares his people's life of trust, and those he saves are his children, as Isaiah's sons were his signs. Qavah, "look to, hope for", is the verb of 40:31, "those who wait for the LORD".

a: the children the LORD has given me
p: Isaiah's sons carry messages in their names, and so does Isaiah: "the LORD saves".
b: Shear-jashub, "a remnant will return" (7:3), and Maher-shalal-hash-baz, "quick to the plunder" (8:1–4), walked the streets of Jerusalem as living signs. Isaiah's own name, Yesha'yahu, means "the LORD saves". Together they tell the whole message: plunder is coming, a remnant will return, the LORD saves. Many readers add Immanuel, "God is with us". "Omens" (mofetim) are signs that point to what is coming, as in 20:3, where Isaiah walks barefoot as "a sign and an omen".

a: the ghosts of the dead and the spirits that know things
p: In a crisis people turned to mediums, who made the dead seem to speak in birdlike whispers.
b: 'Ovot are ghosts (or the pits through which they were called up), and yidde'onim are "knowing ones", spirits said to know the future. The law forbade consulting them (Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:11), and Saul's visit to the woman at Endor is the famous case (1 Samuel 28). The mediums "chirp and mutter": the voices of the dead were thought to be faint and thin, like a bird's (29:4). Ahaz's grandson Manasseh "appointed people to deal with ghosts of the dead and spirits that know things" (2 Kings 21:6). Isaiah's question is scornful: ask the dead about the living? The KJV's "familiar spirits" and "wizards that peep, and that mutter" are older English for the same words.

a: will see no dawn
p: A hard line. It probably means that those who reject the prophet's word have no future, no morning after the night.
b: Literally "which has no dawn (shachar) for it". The KJV has "there is no light in them". The words may describe the people who keep consulting mediums: their night will not end (8:22). Or they may describe the mediums' answers: worthless, "without dawn". Some read shachar as "magic, power to charm" (47:11). The image prepares for 9:2, where the people in darkness see a great light.
orig: אשר אין לו שחר ('asher 'en lo shachar)

a: curse their king and their God
p: Elohav can be "their God" or "their gods"; malko may be "their king" or the god Molech.
b: The starving people blame heaven and their rulers. "Their king and their God" are the two the law says not to curse (Exodus 22:28; 1 Kings 21:10). Some read "their gods", the idols that failed them, and some think malko hints at Molech, a god Judah worshiped later (2 Kings 23:10). The Great Isaiah Scroll has a singular, "his God" (uve'lohu). The Greek has "the ruler and the ancestral things". "They will look up": prayers and curses go upward, but no answer comes.

a: Yet the land that was in distress will not be left in gloom.
p: English 9:1 is the last verse of chapter 8 in Hebrew Bibles, so English 9:2–21 is Hebrew 9:1–20.
b: Hebrew Bibles number this verse 8:23 and begin chapter 9 with "The people walking in the dark". The Greek and Latin Bibles, and English versions after them, start chapter 9 one verse earlier, so every verse to the end of the chapter is one number higher in English: English 9:6 is Hebrew 9:5, and English 9:21 is Hebrew 9:20. This site uses the English numbers throughout. The verse is a hinge: it closes the darkness of 8:21–22 and opens the light of 9:2.

a: he will give weight to
p: Two opposite verbs, qalal ("make light") and kaved ("make heavy"), mean shame and honor, or a light and a heavy blow.
b: Heqal means "made light of, treated with contempt", and hikhbid "made heavy", which can mean "gave honor" (as kavod, "glory", is "weight") or "made the burden heavier". The KJV took both as punishment: "lightly afflicted ... more grievously afflict". Most modern readers, Jewish and Christian, take the second as honor, since 9:2–7 is pure hope: the regions Assyria humiliated first will be honored last. The Plain keeps the play on light and weight.

a: Galilee of the nations
p: In 733–732 BC Tiglath-pileser took Galilee, the coast road and Gilead, and made them Assyrian provinces.
b: "Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came and took Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali" (2 Kings 15:29). From Assyrian records scholars reconstruct three new provinces: probably Dor on the coast ("the way of the sea"), Megiddo in Galilee and Gilead "beyond the Jordan". Zebulun and Naphtali were the tribal lands of Galilee. Galil haggoyim, "the circle (district) of the nations", may already have been an old name for a region where many non-Israelites lived; after the deportations it was truer still. The first to fall into darkness are promised the first light.

a: have seen a great light
p: Matthew quotes 9:1–2 when Jesus moves to Capernaum, in the old land of Zebulun and Naphtali.
b: Matthew 4:13–16 says Jesus settled in Capernaum "in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali" to fulfill this word, and quotes 9:1–2: "the people who sat in darkness / saw a great light, / and for those who sat in the land and shadow of death, / a light rose up" (Matthew 4:16). Matthew's text is mixed: 4:15 is closer to the Hebrew than to the Greek of Isaiah, which begins oddly, "Drink this first, act quickly, land of Zebulun", but 4:16 has "the land and shadow of death", the Greek's phrase (in Rahlfs' and Ziegler's text; Swete's Vaticanus lacks "and"), where the Hebrew has only "a land of tsalmavet". Zechariah's song in Luke 1:79 and Jesus' "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12) also echo this verse. Handel set it in Messiah (1742).

a: the land of deep shadow
p: It sounds like "shadow of death" but probably means "deep darkness". The Greek and Matthew have "shadow of death".
b: Tsalmavet was vowelled by the Masoretes as a compound, tsel "shadow" + mavet "death", and the Greek translated it so (skia thanatou), as do the KJV, Matthew 4:16 and Luke 1:79. Many scholars think it comes from a root tslm, "be dark", meaning simply "deep darkness". The Plain uses "deep shadow" as elsewhere on this site (Job 3:5; Psalm 23:4). Either way it is the darkest darkness, here the darkness of conquest and exile.

a: as on Midian's day
p: The victory will be like Gideon's: God breaking a great oppressor with a tiny force, so that the glory is his.
b: "Midian's day" is the night Gideon's three hundred men routed the Midianites with trumpets and torches (Judges 7). God had sent most of Gideon's army home, because "Israel might glorify itself at my expense" (Judges 7:2). 10:26 recalls the same victory, at "Oreb's Rock" (Judges 7:25), and so does Psalm 83:9–11. The yoke, the bar and the slave driver's stick recall Egypt: the noges, "slave driver", is the word of Exodus 3:7.

a: every boot that stomped
p: The word for "boot" appears only here. It is probably borrowed from the Assyrian word for a soldier's laced boot.
b: Se'on, "boot", and the verb so'en, "booted, tramping", are found nowhere else in the Bible. They match the Akkadian shenu, "shoe, boot". Assyrian palace reliefs show soldiers in high laced boots, unlike the sandals of Israel. So the image is pointed: the gear of the occupying army, and the cloaks soaked in blood, will be piled up and burned. Peace means the end of war's equipment, as in 2:4.

a: For a child has been born to us
p: A royal birth or coronation in Isaiah's day, Hezekiah, an ideal king to come, or Jesus.
b: The verbs are perfects, "has been born", "has been given", like news being announced. A royal birth or accession: many scholars read the poem as celebrating the birth or crowning of a Judean king, using court language ("You are my son. This day I have fathered you", Psalm 2:7), and Jewish tradition from the Talmud to Rashi names Hezekiah. A future king: others note that no king of Judah matched it, and read it as Isaiah's picture of the Messiah, as the Targum does. Jesus: Christians from the second century on, and Handel's Messiah, read it of the birth of Christ. The New Testament does not quote 9:6, but Luke 1:32–33 echoes 9:7, and Matthew 4:15–16 quotes 9:1–2.

a: the rule is on his shoulder
p: The yoke on the people's shoulder (9:4) is replaced by the rule on the king's shoulder.
b: Misrah, "rule, dominion", appears only here and in 9:7. The shoulder may refer to a royal robe or sign of office worn there, like the key of David's house laid "on his shoulder" in 22:22. The contrast with 9:4 is deliberate: the bar across the people's shoulders is broken, and the burden of government rests on the new king instead. The KJV's "government" is the old meaning of that word, "ruling", not a state bureaucracy.

a: He has named him
p: The Hebrew verb is active, "and he called his name", with no subject named. Rashi made God the one who names the child.
b: Vayyiqra' shemo is "and he called his name": the subject may be God, the child's father, or an indefinite "one" ("he has been named"). The Plain keeps the active "He has named him" and leaves "he" open, as the Hebrew does; the Greek and the KJV make it passive, "his name is called", and the Great Isaiah Scroll has a future, "and he will call" (see the variant). Rashi takes God as the subject: the One who is a Wonder of a Counselor, the Mighty God, the Everlasting Father, called the child "Prince of Peace", so only the last title is the child's. The 1985 JPS translation renders the whole as one long name made of sentences about God, much as Hezekiah means "the LORD strengthens". Christian readers, and most modern translations, take all four as titles of the child. The Greek has a single title, "Angel of great counsel", which the old Latin Christmas chant Puer natus est uses.

a: Wonder-Counselor, Mighty God
p: The king plans wonders like God, and is called by a title Isaiah uses of the LORD himself in 10:21.
b: Pele' yo'ets is "a wonder of a counselor": his plans are extraordinary. "Wonder" is usually God's (Exodus 15:11; 25:1), and 28:29 says the LORD is "wonderful in counsel". 'El gibbor, "Mighty God", is used of the LORD in 10:21 (and Deuteronomy 10:17; Jeremiah 32:18 have the same words). Christians read it as a sign that the child is divine. Others render it "godlike hero" or "divine warrior", since kings could be addressed in exalted terms ("Your throne, O God", Psalm 45:6), or take it as part of a name praising God. Many scholars compare the throne names given to Egyptian kings at their crowning.
orig: פלא יועץ אל גבור (pele' yo'ets 'el gibbor)

a: Father Forever, Prince of Peace
p: A king was a father to his people. His rule brings shalom, peace and well-being.
b: 'Avi'ad joins 'av, "father", and 'ad, "perpetuity, forever". A good ruler is a "father" to his people (22:21, of Eliakim; Job 29:16). The phrase may also mean "father of booty", since 'ad can mean "plunder" (Genesis 49:27; 33:23), but few take it so. Christians, who confess the Son and not the Father as the child, read "Everlasting Father" as describing his fatherly care for his people forever, not as confusing the persons of the Trinity. Sar shalom, "Prince of Peace": sar is a commander or official; shalom is wholeness and safety, the fruit of the end of war in 9:5.

a: There will be no end to the growth of his rule
t: The closed letter in the middle of a word
p: The first word is written with a final-form mem in the middle. The Talmud read a lost chance in it.
b: Hebrew has two forms of the letter mem: an open one used inside words and a closed one used at the end. In lemarbeh, "to the growth", the standard Hebrew text writes the closed, final mem in the middle of the word, the only such case in the Bible. The Masoretes kept it (the Qere is the normal spelling). The Talmud explains: God wished to make Hezekiah the Messiah and Sennacherib Gog and Magog, but because Hezekiah did not sing a song of praise after his rescue, the mem was closed (Sanhedrin 94a). The Great Isaiah Scroll writes it as two words, lm rbh, with an ordinary mem.

a: on David's throne and over his kingdom
p: The child sits on David's throne forever, as God promised in 2 Samuel 7. Luke's angel echoes this verse.
b: God promised David a son whose throne would be established forever: "Your house and your kingdom will be made secure forever in front of you. Your throne will stand firm for all time" (2 Samuel 7:16). Psalm 89 holds God to that promise when the dynasty failed. Gabriel's words to Mary echo 9:7 closely: "The Lord God will hand him the throne of David his father, and he will be king over Jacob's house for all the ages. His kingdom will have no end" (Luke 1:32–33). "Justice and righteousness" are the two things Isaiah found missing in Jerusalem (5:7).

a: The zeal of the LORD of Armies will make it happen.
p: The same words close Isaiah's promise of a surviving remnant in 37:32, also in 2 Kings 19:31.
b: Qin'ah is passionate commitment, the jealousy of a husband for his wife or a God for his people. The same sentence ends the promise to Hezekiah that "Out of Jerusalem a remnant will go out, / survivors from Mount Zion. / The zeal of the LORD of Armies will make it happen" (2 Kings 19:31; Isaiah 37:32). Not the king's power but God's zeal will bring the kingdom.
orig: קנאת יהוה צבאות תעשה זאת (qin'at YHWH tseva'ot ta'aseh zot)

a: The Lord has sent out a word into Jacob
t: The poem of the outstretched hand
p: 9:8–10:4 is one poem in four stanzas, each ending with the same refrain. Its first stanza may be in 5:25.
b: Each stanza tells a disaster that should have turned Israel back, and ends: "In spite of all this, his anger has not turned back, / and his hand is still stretched out" (9:12, 17, 21; 10:4). The same refrain closes 5:25, and 5:26–30 describes the Assyrian invasion that would make a fitting end. Many scholars think the poem was once one piece, later split when Isaiah's memoir (6:1–9:7) was set in the middle; others think the editor framed the memoir with it on purpose. The poem is aimed at the northern kingdom (9:9), though 10:1–4 turns to Judah's leaders too.

a: We will use cedars instead.
t: A boast and a modern reading
p: Samaria met disaster with pride: we will rebuild bigger. A 2011 Christian novel applied the verse to America after 9/11.
b: Sycamore-fig wood was the cheap building timber of Israel's lowlands (1 Kings 10:27), and dressed stone and cedar the costly materials of palaces. After an earthquake or Assyrian attack, Samaria's leaders vowed to rebuild finer than before, instead of asking why it happened. Jonathan Cahn's novel The Harbinger (2011) reads the verse as a warning to the United States. Cahn argues that America, like Israel, was founded in covenant with God, and that events after September 11, 2001 matched the verse's details: fallen buildings, a sycamore felled at Ground Zero and replaced by a conifer, a quarried stone laid at the site, and a US Senate leader who quoted the verse the next day. Read in its setting, the verse is a judgment on the northern kingdom of Israel in the 700s BC; readers who apply it to other nations use it as an example of national pride.
orig: שקמים גדעו וארזים נחליף (shiqmim gudda'u va'arazim nachalif)

a: Rezin's foes
p: Rezin was Israel's ally, so his foes rising against Israel is odd. Many read "his foes", that is, Israel's.
b: The Hebrew is "the foes of Rezin". If the verse looks back to the time before the alliance, Aram itself had once attacked Israel. Many scholars think Retsin crept in from 8:6 and read tsarav, "his (Israel's) foes". Others suggest it means Assyria, Rezin's great enemy, which turned on Israel too. The Greek has "those rising against Mount Zion". The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: and his hand is still stretched out
t: The outstretched hand turned against Israel
p: The arm that brought Israel out of Egypt is now stretched out against Israel. And the people still do not turn back.
b: "With an outstretched arm" the LORD rescued Israel from Egypt (Exodus 6:6; Deuteronomy 4:34). Here the same gesture threatens. The refrain also plays on shuv, "turn back": his anger "has not turned back" (9:12) because the people "have not turned back" to him (9:13). In 12:1 the redeemed will finally sing "let your anger turn back".

a: the Philistines from the west
p: Aram attacked from the east and the Philistines from the west. The Greek calls them "the Greeks".
b: Hebrew "from the front" (miqqedem) and "from behind" (me'achor) mean east and west for someone facing sunrise. Aram had raided Israel for a century (2 Kings 13:3–7), and the Philistines raided the lowlands of Judah in Ahaz's day (2 Chronicles 28:18). The Greek of Isaiah, made in the Hellenistic age, translates "Philistines" as "the Greeks", the coastal peoples of its own time.

a: The head means the elder and the man of rank
p: Many scholars think this verse is an early reader's note explaining 9:14. It also targets false prophets.
b: 9:14 uses proverbial pairs for "everyone": head and tail, the palm branch at the top of the tree and the rush in the swamp. 9:15 explains the pairs narrowly, as the leaders and the lying prophets, which fits poorly with the next line. Many scholars, from Duhm on, take it as a gloss written into the text; others think Isaiah himself is turning the saying against the elite. Either way the point stands: a nation's leaders and its false teachers share the blame (Micah 3:5–11).

a: engulfed
p: Bala' means "swallow" and also "confuse, throw into chaos". Both fit a people misled by its leaders.
b: The same word appears in 3:12, "those who lead you mislead you, and confuse the course of your paths", and in 19:3 and 28:7. Isaiah says the leaders me'ashsherim, literally "those who keep this people going straight", have done the opposite: mat'im, "lead astray". The guided are lost, swallowed up in the confusion.

a: the land is burned black
p: Ne'tam is found only here. The Greek has "burned up"; the KJV has "darkened". The Plain keeps both fire and dark.
b: Ne'tam appears nowhere else in the Bible, and its meaning is guessed from context and related languages. Many take it as "scorched", which fits the fire of 9:18–19; the Greek has "the whole land is burned up". The KJV, "is the land darkened", follows an older guess. The Great Isaiah Scroll writes the letters in another order (nt'm), perhaps a scribe's attempt at a rare word. The Plain's "burned black" keeps both senses: a land on fire and a land left in smoke and darkness.

a: the flesh of his own arm
p: A picture of famine and civil war: a people devouring itself. Some read "his neighbor's flesh".
b: "Every man eats the flesh of his own arm": in starvation people turn on their own. The Great Isaiah Scroll (zrw'w, "his arm") and the Greek ("of his arm") agree with the Masoretic Text; 4QIsa-e writes zr'yw, which can be read "his offspring" or a plural, "his arms". Many scholars change the vowels of zero'o, "his arm", to zar'o, "his offspring", or read re'o, "his neighbor". The next verse explains it as civil war: Manasseh against Ephraim. Israel's last decades saw four of its kings assassinated (2 Kings 15:10–30).

a: Manasseh feeds on Ephraim, Ephraim on Manasseh
p: Manasseh and Ephraim, Joseph's two sons, were the core of the northern kingdom. Its last years were a series of coups.
b: Shallum killed Zechariah, Menahem killed Shallum, Pekah killed Pekahiah and Hoshea killed Pekah, all within about twenty years (2 Kings 15:10–30). Pekah came to power from Gilead, Manasseh's land east of the Jordan: "Fifty men of the Gileadites were with Pekah" (2 Kings 15:25). The two brother tribes "feed on" each other and agree only in attacking Judah, as in the war of 7:1.

a: Woe to those who lay down wicked rules
p: 10:1–4 matches the six woes of 5:8–23 and may once have stood with them: the final woe is on corrupt lawmakers.
b: Isaiah's woes in 5:8–23 target land-grabbers, drunkards, scoffers and corrupt judges. This seventh woe is against officials who write unjust law itself: decrees that make theft legal. The prophets saw legal oppression as worse than crime because it uses God's gift of law against the weak (Amos 5:7; Micah 3:9–11). "Rules" (chuqqim) is the word for God's statutes in the law; here human officials decree their own.
orig: הוי החקקים חקקי און (hoy hachoqeqim chiqqeqe 'aven)

a: so that widows become their loot
p: Widows and the fatherless had no man to plead for them. The law put them under God's own protection.
b: "Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly" (Exodus 22:22) carries a threat: God himself will hear their cry and act (Exodus 22:23–24). Isaiah's first chapter called Jerusalem to "plead the widow's case" (1:17), and its leaders failed (1:23). Here the officials "loot" the very people the law protected. The words for loot and plunder, shalal and baz, are the words in Maher-shalal-hash-baz's name (8:1): those who plunder the poor will be plundered by Assyria (10:6).

a: the day of accounting
p: Pequddah is God's "visit" to set accounts right: for the oppressor, the day of punishment.
b: The root paqad means to visit, inspect, take account of; it can bring care (Genesis 21:1, "the LORD visited Sarah") or punishment. The KJV's "day of visitation" keeps the word. The same root returns in 10:12, "I will bring to account" the king of Assyria: the God who will judge Judah's officials will also judge the empire he uses against them. The question "where will you stash your riches?" (literally "your glory") mocks those who gained wealth by injustice.

a: You can only crouch beneath the prisoners
t: An obscure line and a famous guess
p: The Hebrew is hard. A nineteenth-century scholar found two foreign gods in it; most now keep the text.
b: Literally "except one has crouched under (the) prisoner, and under the slain they will fall". The sense seems to be: there is nowhere to hide except among the captives and the dead. Paul de Lagarde redivided the letters to read "Beltis crouches, Osiris is shattered", the gods of Babylon and Egypt, and some scholars followed him. Most commentators today reject the emendation and read the line as it stands. The refrain then closes the poem that began at 9:8.
orig: בלתי כרע תחת אסיר (bilti kara' tachat 'assir)

a: Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger
p: God uses Assyria to punish his people, and then holds Assyria to account for its pride and cruelty.
b: Isaiah makes a bold claim: the empire that terrified the world was a stick in God's hand. The same idea runs through the prophets: Babylon's king is "my servant" (Jeremiah 25:9), Cyrus is "my anointed" (45:1), and the Chaldeans are raised up to punish (Habakkuk 1:6). But being a tool does not make Assyria innocent. It meant to destroy, not to correct (10:7), and it boasted (10:13–14). Jewish and Christian interpreters have read the passage as a key to how God rules history: he governs even the acts of those who do not know him, without approving their evil. Others question whether any empire's violence can be called God's work.

a: It is a stick, and my rage is in their hand.
p: The Hebrew reads, word for word, "and a staff it, in their hand my fury". The little word "it" is hard to place.
b: The line runs umatteh hu' veyadam za'mi. Read as it stands, hu', "it", makes Assyria the subject: "it is a staff", the LORD's weapon, with his fury in its soldiers' hands. Many scholars take hu' as a later gloss or a slip and read "the staff in their hand is my fury". The Great Isaiah Scroll has the same words as the Masoretic Text. The Greek has "the rod of my wrath, and the anger is in their hands", with no staff. On every reading, Assyria's weapons carry the LORD's anger, not its own (10:15).
orig: ומטה הוא בידם זעמי (umatteh hu' veyadam za'mi)

a: a godless nation
p: The "godless nation" that Assyria is sent against is God's own people.
b: Goy chanef: chanef means godless, polluted, a hypocrite (9:17; 33:14). Calling Judah a goy, the ordinary word for a foreign nation, rather than 'am, "people", stings (compare 1:4, "sinful nation"). "The people I am angry with" is literally "the people of my wrath". The verbs of plunder are again those of Maher-shalal-hash-baz's name (8:1).

a: Calno went the way of Carchemish, didn't it?
p: Every city in the list fell to Assyria between 740 and 717 BC, from north Syria down to Samaria.
b: Arpad fell to Tiglath-pileser in 740 BC, Calno (Kullani) in 738, Hamath was crushed by 738 and again by Sargon in 720, Damascus in 732, Samaria in 722, and Carchemish, the great city on the Euphrates, to Sargon in 717. The pairs move from north to south, toward Jerusalem. Since Carchemish fell last, the speech fits the time of Sargon or Sennacherib, after 717. The Assyrian envoy uses the same boast to Hezekiah: "Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad?" (36:19; 37:13).

a: the kingdoms of the worthless idols
t: To Assyria all gods were alike
p: The Assyrian calls the gods of other kingdoms 'elilim, "worthless idols", and counts Jerusalem's God among them.
b: 'Elilim is Isaiah's mocking word for idols, a pun on 'elohim, "gods", and 'al, "nothing" (2:8). Put in the Assyrian's mouth, it shows his view: the gods of Samaria and Jerusalem are no different from those of the cities he has already taken. He has more images to boast of conquering. The irony is that the reader knows Jerusalem's God is the one using him. The same argument appears in 36:18–20.

a: I will bring to account
p: The verse starts by speaking of the Lord and switches to "I". The Greek smooths it to "he".
b: Hebrew prophecy often moves between the prophet's words about God and God's own words, and readers are expected to follow the change. Here "the Lord" finishes his work, and then "I" punish. The Greek has "he will bring". Some versions add "he will say". "The fruit of the swollen heart" is the boastful talk of 10:8–11 and 10:13–14; "the proud glory of his lofty eyes" is his arrogance (2:11). The "work on Mount Zion" is God's purifying judgment on Jerusalem (1:24–26), after which he will turn on the tool he used.

a: I did this with my own strong hand
t: The voice of the Assyrian kings
p: Isaiah's Assyrian talks like the real kings' inscriptions: my strength, my wisdom, borders moved, peoples carried off.
b: Assyrian royal annals boast in the first person of the king's strength and wisdom, of cities taken and plundered, and of peoples deported and resettled, "counted with the people of Assyria". Tiglath-pileser III began mass deportation as a policy; "I wiped out the borders between peoples" describes it exactly. Peter Machinist has shown how closely Isaiah's speeches for the Assyrian echo the empire's own propaganda, and turn it inside out. The Assyrian credits himself; Isaiah credits God (10:15).

a: Can an ax take credit over the man who chops with it?
p: An ax boasting against the woodsman is absurd. So is Assyria boasting against God.
b: The pictures pile up: ax, saw, rod, staff. Each is lifeless wood or iron that moves only when someone lifts it. Paul uses a similar picture of the potter and clay, drawn from 29:16 and 45:9, to say that God's purposes do not answer to his creatures (Romans 9:20–21). The verse closes Isaiah's argument against Assyria's pride and leads into its punishment.

a: will send leanness into his well-fed men
p: The fat warriors will waste away. Readers have connected it with the disaster at Jerusalem in 701 BC.
b: Mishmannav, "his fat ones", are the well-fed soldiers or nobles; razon, "leanness", a wasting disease. 37:36 and 2 Kings 19:35 tell how the angel of the LORD struck down 185,000 Assyrians outside Jerusalem, and Herodotus (2.141) has a story of mice gnawing the bowstrings of Sennacherib's army in Egypt, which some take as a memory of plague. Whatever happened, Sennacherib went home without taking Jerusalem. The fire "under his glory" burns from inside, like fever.

a: Israel's Light will turn into fire
p: The God who is Israel's light becomes a fire that burns Assyria's thorns in one day.
b: "The LORD is my light" (Psalm 27:1), and he is also "a consuming fire" (Deuteronomy 4:24; Hebrews 12:29). He met Moses in a bush that burned and was not consumed (Exodus 3:2). Here the light turns to fire against the enemy: Assyria's army, a forest and a thornbush ("his thornbush and his bramble") that seemed endless, burns in a single day. "Its Holy One" is Isaiah's "Holy One of Israel".

a: it will be like a sick man wasting away
t: A sick man, or a standard-bearer?
p: Kimsos noses is found only here. Most read "as a sick man wastes away"; the KJV has "as when a standardbearer fainteth".
b: The two Hebrew words sound alike, kimsos noses, and neither appears elsewhere in this form. Most scholars take them from roots meaning "melt, waste away" and "be sick": the Assyrian army will waste away like a man with a fatal illness, as the "leanness" of 10:16 had said. The KJV, "as when a standardbearer fainteth", connected noses with nes, "flag". The Greek reads the line differently: "the one fleeing will be like one fleeing from a burning flame". The Great Isaiah Scroll and 1QIsa-b have the same words as the Masoretic Text.

a: the remnant of Israel, the survivors of Jacob's house
p: Ahaz leaned on Assyria, the power that then beat Judah. The survivors will lean on God.
b: She'ar is "remnant" and peletah "survivors, those who escaped". "The one who beat them" is Assyria: Ahaz had called it in (2 Kings 16:7), and it became Judah's oppressor. Nish'an, "lean on", is the word of 30:12 and 31:1, where Judah leans on Egypt instead. The remnant will "truly" (be'emet, "in faithfulness") lean on the Holy One of Israel, the trust Ahaz refused in 7:9.
orig: שאר ישראל ופליטת בית יעקב (she'ar Yisra'el ufletat bet Ya'aqov)

a: A remnant will return, Jacob's remnant, to the Mighty God.
p: The words of Shear-jashub's name come back as a promise: a remnant will return to God.
b: She'ar yashuv is exactly the name of Isaiah's son (7:3). "Return" (shuv) means both coming home and repenting, turning back to God, the turning the refrain of 9:12–10:4 said Israel refused. "The Mighty God", 'el gibbor, is the title of the child in 9:6, now plainly used of God himself, which Christian readers take as support for the divine reading of 9:6 and others as showing that the child's name praised God.
orig: שאר ישוב (she'ar yashuv); אל גבור ('el gibbor)

a: Even if your people, Israel, were like the sand of the sea
p: Paul quotes these verses in their Greek form: only a remnant will be saved.
b: God promised Abraham descendants as many as "the sand on the seashore" (Genesis 22:17). Isaiah says the number will not save them: only a remnant will return. Paul quotes the Greek of 10:22–23 in Romans 9:27–28: "Isaiah cries out about Israel: 'Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, only the remnant will be saved. For the Lord will carry out his sentence on the earth, finishing it and cutting it short.'" The Greek has "will be saved" for "will return", and its "cutting short" reads the Hebrew "settled end" as a sentence carried out quickly. Paul uses it to say that in his own day too, a remnant of Israel believes (Romans 11:5).

a: a settled end
p: Kalah venecheratsah is a fixed phrase for a final, decreed destruction, used again in 28:22 and in Daniel.
b: Kalah is a complete end; necheratsah "something cut, decided". The pair returns in 28:22, where Isaiah has heard of such an end from the Lord GOD of Armies, and in Daniel 9:27 and 11:36, which take up Isaiah's words about the end of the wicked king. In 10:22 the destruction "floods in with righteousness": the judgment is just, and it makes room for the remnant.

a: the way it was done in Egypt
t: A new Egypt, a new exodus
p: Assyria beats Judah as Egypt beat Israel. So the LORD will rescue them as he did at the sea.
b: Bederekh Mitsrayim, "in the way of Egypt", frames 10:24–26: Assyria's rod is like the slave drivers' (Exodus 5:14), and the LORD's staff will be raised over the sea as Moses' was (Exodus 14:16, 26). Isaiah often tells the future through the exodus: a new deliverance, a road through the sea (11:15–16; 43:16–19; 51:9–11). The "little while" (10:25) promises the oppression will be short.

a: Oreb's Rock
p: The Ephraimites killed Oreb, a Midianite prince, at a rock named after him, in Gideon's war.
b: After Gideon's night attack, the men of Ephraim caught the two Midianite commanders: "They killed Oreb at the Rock of Oreb, and Zeeb they killed at the Winepress of Zeeb" (Judges 7:25). Like "Midian's day" in 9:4, it recalls a victory where God saved Israel against great odds, with a small band. The verse joins two victories: Gideon's over Midian and Moses' at the sea, where Moses raised his staff (Exodus 14:16).

a: The yoke will snap because of fatness.
p: The Hebrew is obscure. The KJV's "because of the anointing" became a favorite text in some churches.
b: Mippene shamen literally means "from before fat (or oil)". Readings: the ox has grown so fat that the yoke breaks; the yoke rots from oil; or the text is damaged. The KJV has "the yoke shall be destroyed because of the anointing", and the Targum also finds the Anointed One, the Messiah, in the verse. The KJV phrase is much used in Pentecostal and charismatic preaching for the power of the Spirit. Many scholars join the last words to 10:28 and emend them to a place name, "he has come up from Rimmon" or "from Samaria" or "from Jeshimon", starting the enemy's march. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and its uncertainty.
orig: וחבל על מפני שמן (vechubbal 'ol mippene shamen)

a: He has reached Aiath
p: Town by town, an enemy army closes in on Jerusalem from the north, to within sight of the city.
b: The towns run from Aiath (Ai, near Bethel) through Michmash and the pass to Geba, where Jonathan once fought the Philistines (1 Samuel 13–14), past Ramah, Gibeah of Saul and Anathoth, to Nob, on the ridge just north of Jerusalem (1 Samuel 21–22). The route avoids the main road and takes a hard shortcut through the pass. Whose army? Assyria's under Sargon or Sennacherib, though Sennacherib came from the southwest in 701; the Aramean-Israelite army of 734; or a poetic picture of the dreaded attack. Either way, at the last moment the LORD cuts the forest down (10:33–34).
r: 1 Samuel 13:23–14:5; 1 Samuel 21:1; 1 Samuel 22:19; Joshua 21:18; Jeremiah 1:1; Nehemiah 11:31–32

a: Poor Anathoth!
p: The names chime with the verbs: Gallim with galli "wail", Anathoth with 'aniyyah "poor" or 'aneha "answer her".
b: Isaiah makes the place names part of the panic. "Cry out, daughter Gallim" (tsahali bat Gallim); "Listen, Laishah" (haqshivi Layshah); "Poor Anathoth" ('aniyyah 'Anatot). Some change the vowels to 'aniha, "answer her, Anathoth". Anathoth, a town of priests, was later Jeremiah's home (Jeremiah 1:1). "Daughter" before a town name is a fond or pitying way to speak of its people.

a: is hacking off the boughs with a frightful crash
p: Assyria, which boasted of cutting the cedars of Lebanon, is itself chopped down like a forest.
b: The Assyrian kings bragged of felling the cedars of Lebanon for their palaces, and Sennacherib boasts of it in 37:24. Isaiah turns the picture on him: the Lord fells the proud trees. Then chapter 11 begins with a stump that sprouts. The great forest of Assyria falls and does not grow again; the stump of Jesse, cut down too, puts out a shoot (11:1). The contrast between the two felled trees is the hinge between the chapters.

a: Lebanon will fall to a mighty one
t: Lebanon and the Branch at Qumran
p: Who is the "mighty one", God or an army? The Dead Sea community read 10:34–11:1 as a prophecy of their own war.
b: Be'addir, "by a mighty one", may be the LORD (33:21; Psalm 93:4) or the mighty trees, or an army. The Qumran commentary on Isaiah (4Q161) applies 10:22–11:5 to the last war, when "the Branch of David" will rise. Another scroll (4Q285) quotes 10:34–11:1 and speaks of the Branch of David and the Prince of the Congregation killing the leader of the Kittim, probably the Romans. So by the first century BC, Jews were reading the fall of Lebanon and the shoot of Jesse as one event in the coming age.

a: From Jesse's stump a shoot will come out
p: David's family tree will be cut down to a stump, but a new shoot will grow from it.
b: Geza' is the stump left after a tree is felled (40:24), and Job says that even a felled tree has hope of new growth (Job 14:7–9). Isaiah names Jesse, not David: the new king will come from the roots of the family, as if the line had to start over, the way David himself was the youngest son of a Bethlehem farmer (1 Samuel 16:1–13). The image follows the felling of Assyria's forest (10:33–34) and picks up the "holy seed" in the stump of 6:13. The Targum makes it plain: a king will come from the sons of Jesse, and the Messiah will be exalted (or anointed) from his sons' sons.

a: a sprout
p: Netser means a green shoot. Many think Matthew's "He will be called a Nazarene" plays on it.
b: Netser is a fresh shoot (14:19; 60:21). Jeremiah and Zechariah use a different word, tsemach, for the "Branch" of David (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8). Since Jerome, many have connected netser with Nazareth (Hebrew Natsrat) and with Matthew 2:23: "He will be called a Nazarene." The Greek has "a flower will come up from the root", and Jerome's Latin, "a rod (virga) will come out of the root of Jesse, and a flower (flos) will rise from his root". Jerome's commentary reads the rod as the Virgin Mary (virgo) and the flower as Christ, the image behind the carol "Lo, How a Rose E'er Blooming".

a: The LORD's Spirit will come to rest on him
p: The Hebrew names six qualities in three pairs. The Greek and Latin have seven: the "seven gifts of the Holy Spirit".
b: The Hebrew lists the Spirit of the LORD and then three pairs: wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and fear of the LORD. The Greek translates the last "fear" as eusebeia, "godliness", and then opens 11:3 with "the spirit of the fear of God will fill him", making seven; the Latin follows, with pietas and timor Domini. From this came the church's teaching on the seven gifts: "wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord" (Catechism of the Catholic Church 1831), set out by Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I–II, question 68). Revelation's "seven spirits" before the throne (Revelation 1:4) may also draw on it. See "Where Christians differ" on the chapter page.
orig: רוח חכמה ובינה רוח עצה וגבורה רוח דעת ויראת יהוה

a: a spirit of wisdom and understanding
t: The gifts of a good king
p: The qualities are those of Israel's best leaders: Solomon's wisdom, David's strength, and the fear of the LORD.
b: God gave Solomon "a heart that is wise and understanding" (1 Kings 3:12); Bezalel was filled "with the Spirit of God, with skill, with understanding, with know-how" (Exodus 31:3); the elders of Moses shared his spirit (Numbers 11:17). "Counsel and strength" recall the Wonder-Counselor and Mighty God of 9:6. Later Jewish texts give the coming king these gifts: Psalms of Solomon 17:37, 1 Enoch 49:3 (of the Chosen One) and the Qumran blessing of the Prince of the Congregation (1QSb 5:24–25). At Jesus' baptism the Spirit comes down and "stays" on him (John 1:32–33; Matthew 3:16).
r: 1 Kings 3:12; Exodus 31:3; Numbers 11:17; 9:6; 1 Enoch 49:3; John 1:32–33; Matthew 3:16; Luke 4:18

a: The fear of the LORD will be a sweet smell to him
p: The verb means "smell": he will delight in the fear of the LORD as in a fragrance. The Talmud took it literally.
b: Vahariycho is from riach, "smell", used of God smelling a pleasing sacrifice (Genesis 8:21) or refusing to (Amos 5:21). Most versions say "he will delight"; the KJV, "shall make him of quick understanding", took it as keen perception, a quick "scent". The Talmud reads it as a sign of the Messiah: he will "smell and judge", knowing the truth without witnesses. It tells that Bar Koziba (Bar Kokhba, who led the revolt against Rome in AD 132–135) was tested this way and failed (Sanhedrin 93b). The next lines say the same: he will not judge by appearances or hearsay (compare 1 Samuel 16:7; John 7:24).

a: His mouth will be a rod to strike the earth
p: The king's word is his rod. Paul and Revelation take the picture up for Christ's coming in judgment.
b: The king of Psalm 2 breaks the nations "with an iron rod" (Psalm 2:9); this king's rod is his mouth. Psalms of Solomon 17:24 combines the two for the Messiah. Paul says the lawless one will be revealed, "whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth" (2 Thessalonians 2:8), and Revelation pictures Christ: "A sharp sword comes out of his mouth to strike down the nations" (Revelation 19:15). Some scholars read 'arits, "the ruthless", for 'erets, "the earth", to match "the wicked" in the next line.

a: He will wear righteousness as the band around his waist
p: A belt holds the clothes for work or battle. His belt is righteousness and faithfulness.
b: The ezor was a waist-band or loincloth, tied tight before action (1 Kings 18:46). God himself puts on righteousness as armor in 59:17, and Paul tells believers to stand with "the belt of truth" and "the breastplate of righteousness" (Ephesians 6:14), using both passages. "Faithfulness" ('emunah) is from the same root as "hold firm" in 7:9: the king is what Ahaz was not.

a: The wolf will stay as a guest with the lamb
p: Read literally, as creation restored, or as a picture of peace between the nations, or both.
b: Predators and prey live together, and children play where snakes were. Literal readings: Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.33.4) took it of the coming kingdom on a renewed earth, and many premillennial Christians read it of Christ's thousand-year reign; others read it of the new creation (65:17–25). Figurative readings: Maimonides wrote that "the wolf and the lamb" is a parable, meaning Israel will live safely among nations once fierce as wolves (Mishneh Torah, Kings 12:1); many Christians read it of the gospel making enemies into family. Many readers hold both: the peace of the Messiah's rule reaches all creation (Romans 8:19–22). The picture reverses the fear of Genesis 9:2 and recalls Eden (Genesis 1:29–30). 65:25 repeats part of it.
r: 65:25; Genesis 1:29–30; Genesis 9:2; Hosea 2:18; Ezekiel 34:25; Romans 8:19–22; Revelation 20:4–6

a: a small boy will herd them
p: The child who leads the animals recalls the children who are signs in 7–9 and the child-king of 9:6.
b: Na'ar qaton, "a little boy", drives (noheg) them like a shepherd with a flock. In chapters 7–11 children carry the hope: Immanuel (7:14), Isaiah's sons (8:18), the child born to us (9:6). Here a child does what kings and armies could not: he leads without force. Readers have also linked it with Jesus' teaching that the kingdom belongs to children (Mark 10:14–15).
orig: ונער קטן נהג בם (vena'ar qaton noheg bam)

a: the lion, like the ox, will eat straw
p: The popular saying "the lion shall lie down with the lamb" is not in the Bible. Isaiah pairs the wolf with the lamb.
b: The familiar line about the lion and the lamb blends two images. In Isaiah the wolf stays with the lamb and the leopard beds down with the young goat (11:6); the lion is beside the calf and eats straw like the ox (11:6–7). 65:25 repeats the scene: wolf and lamb graze together and the lion eats straw like the ox. The lion's new diet is the point: the predator is changed, not merely restrained.

a: a viper's lair
p: The KJV's "asp" and "cockatrice" are old names for real snakes; the cockatrice was a mythical one.
b: Peten is probably the cobra and tsif'oni a viper. The KJV's "cockatrice" was a fabled creature, half rooster and half serpent, whose look could kill; the translators used the word for an unknown deadly snake. Me'urah, "lair", is found only here; it may be a hole, or literally "a place of light", the snake's peephole. The weaned child (about three years old) puts his hand where any parent would snatch it away.
orig: חר פתן ... מאורת צפעוני (chur peten ... me'urat tsif'oni)

a: like waters covering the sea
t: Knowing the LORD fills the earth
p: Habakkuk 2:14 repeats the line with "the glory of the LORD". 65:25 repeats the line before it.
b: Habakkuk 2:14 says the earth will be filled "with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea". One Qumran copy of Isaiah (4QIsa-c) has "glory" here too (see the variant). "My holy mountain" is Zion (2:2–4; 65:25): peace begins at the LORD's dwelling and spreads to the whole earth. De'ah 'et YHWH is "knowing the LORD", the relationship that Hosea says Israel lacked (Hosea 4:1, 6) and that Jeremiah's new covenant promises to all (Jeremiah 31:34).
orig: דעה את יהוה כמים לים מכסים (de'ah 'et YHWH kammayim layyam mekhassim)

a: the root of Jesse
p: Paul quotes the Greek of this verse: the nations will hope in him. Revelation calls Jesus "the Root of David".
b: The Greek has: "there will be the root of Jesse, and the one who rises to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope". Paul quotes it in Romans 15:12 to close his argument that the Gentiles praise God with Israel: "The root of Jesse will come, the one who rises to rule the nations; the nations will put their hope in him." Revelation 5:5 calls Jesus "the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David", and in Revelation 22:16 he says, "I am the Root and the Descendant of David". In 11:1 the king grew from the root; here he is the root, the source of the family itself.

a: a flag for the peoples
p: A nes is a pole with a banner on a hill to rally troops. Here it gathers the nations to the king.
b: In 5:26 the LORD raises a flag to summon a foreign army against Israel; here and in 11:12 the flag summons the nations and the exiles home (also 49:22; 62:10). The same word names the pole on which Moses set the bronze serpent: "Make yourself a burning one and put it on a pole" (Numbers 21:8), and John 3:14 compares Jesus' lifting up on the cross to it. Isaiah's flag stands "for the peoples", not only for Israel.

a: the place where he rests will be glory
t: His resting place, or his tomb?
p: Menuchah is a place of rest, used of the Temple. Jerome's Latin has "his tomb will be glorious".
b: Menuchah is rest or a resting place: the LORD calls Zion "my place of rest forever and ever" (Psalm 132:14), and the ark sought a resting place (Numbers 10:33). So the verse may mean that the king's dwelling, Jerusalem, will be full of glory, or that his peace will be glorious. The Greek has "his rest will be honor". Jerome translated et erit sepulchrum eius gloriosum, "and his tomb will be glorious", and medieval Christians read it of the empty tomb of Christ; the Hebrew does not say "tomb".

a: a second time
p: The first time the LORD brought his people out of Egypt. Now he will bring them home from every direction.
b: "A second time" looks back to the exodus (11:16). The list covers the known world: Assyria and Egypt; Pathros (Upper Egypt) and Cush (Nubia, south of Egypt); Elam (east of Babylonia) and Shinar (the old name for Babylonia, Genesis 11:2); Hamath in Syria; and "the islands of the sea", the Mediterranean coasts. "Claim as his own" (qanah, "acquire, make one's own") is the verb of the Song of the Sea: "until this people you have made your own cross over" (Exodus 15:16). Many scholars date 11:10–16 after the exile, when Jews were in fact scattered this widely; others hold that Isaiah foresaw it, since Assyria had already deported Israelites far and wide (2 Kings 17:6).

a: Judah's scattered ones
p: A masculine form for Israel's outcasts and a feminine one for Judah's scattered: together, the whole people.
b: Nidche Yisra'el, "the driven-out of Israel", is masculine, and nefutsot Yehudah, "the scattered of Judah", is feminine. Hebrew poetry often splits a whole into two parts: here north and south, and perhaps men and women, meaning the whole people. The Plain does not mark the genders, which would suggest that only women of Judah were scattered. "The four corners of the earth" are literally "the four wings (edges) of the earth", the farthest places in every direction (Ezekiel 7:2; Revelation 7:1). The daily Jewish Amidah draws on this verse when it asks God to raise a flag to gather the exiles "from the four corners of the earth".
orig: נדחי ישראל ונפצות יהודה (nidche Yisra'el unefutsot Yehudah)

a: The envy of Ephraim will be gone
p: The two kingdoms had been rivals since Jeroboam. The prophets hoped for one people again under David's line.
b: Ephraim's jealousy of Judah went back to the judges (Judges 8:1; 12:1) and split the kingdom after Solomon (1 Kings 12). In Isaiah's day the north had just attacked Judah (7:1). The prophets foresaw an end to it: Ezekiel joins two sticks, Judah and Joseph, into one (Ezekiel 37:15–22), and Hosea sees the people of Judah and Israel gathered under one head (Hosea 1:11). "Judah's harassers" may be Judah's enemies or Judah's own hostility; the next line points to the second: neither side will harass the other.

a: the shoulder of the Philistines to the west
p: The "shoulder" is the slope of the Philistine hills. The reunited people swoop down on old enemies like birds of prey.
b: Katef, "shoulder", means a hill slope, probably the low hills toward the Philistine coast; Joshua 15:8 uses it of a ridge. The verb ('af) means to fly or swoop, like birds of prey. The neighbors who raided Israel in Isaiah's day (9:12; 2 Chronicles 28:17–18) are now subject to it, as in David's reign. Many readers find this hard beside 11:6–9: some see a picture of security in ancient terms, some a later addition, and others read it figuratively.

a: The LORD will lay waste the tongue of Egypt's sea
p: The verb is cherem, "devote to destruction". Many read a near-identical verb, "dry up", as the Greek may have.
b: Hecherim is the verb of cherem, the "ban" on things devoted to destruction (Joshua 6:17). A sea cannot be under the ban in that sense, so the Plain says "lay waste".
