Many scholars read hecheriv, "dry up" (one letter different), which fits the crossing "in sandals", and the Greek has "will make desolate". "The tongue" is a gulf, probably the Gulf of Suez. "The River" is the Euphrates, split into seven gullies as the Red Sea was split. The burning wind ('ayam, found only here) recalls the east wind of Exodus 14:21. Revelation 16:12 pictures the Euphrates dried up for the kings from the east.

a: There will be a road raised up
p: A mesillah is a built-up road. Isaiah's book is full of them: the road home from exile is the road of the new exodus.
b: A mesillah is a raised road, graded and cleared. The word returns at key points of the book: a highway from Egypt to Assyria (19:23), the Holy Way for the redeemed (35:8), the road in the wilderness (40:3), the roads raised up for the returning exiles (49:11; 62:10). Even the road where Isaiah met Ahaz, "the main road to the Launderers' Field" (7:3), is a mesillah. The road Ahaz walked in unbelief becomes, at the end of these chapters, the road of God's people coming home.

a: On that day you will say
t: A new Song of the Sea
p: After the new exodus of 11:15–16 comes a song, as the Song of the Sea followed the crossing in Exodus 15.
b: Moses and Israel sang after the crossing (Exodus 15:1–18), and Miriam led the women (Exodus 15:20–21). Chapter 12 is the song for the second crossing, and it quotes Exodus 15:2 (12:2). The "you" of 12:1 is singular, as if the redeemed people sang with one voice; in 12:3–4 it is plural. The song closes the first part of the book (1–12), which opened with a people in rebellion (1:2–4) and ends with the Holy One of Israel in their midst (12:6).

a: now let your anger turn back
p: The refrain of 9:12–10:4 said his anger "has not turned back". Here, at last, it does.
b: The Hebrew yashov appekha is a wish, "may your anger turn back", or, read with different vowels, a past, "your anger turned back" (as in the Greek, the KJV and most versions). The Plain follows the Masoretic vowels. Either way, the words answer the refrain "his anger has not turned back" (9:12, 17, 21; 10:4; 5:25), with the same verb, shuv. Comfort (nicham) is the keyword of 40:1, where the second half of the book begins.

a: my strength and my song is Yah, the LORD
p: The line is the Song of the Sea word for word, with God's name doubled: Yah, the LORD.
b: Exodus 15:2 and Psalm 118:14 read: "My strength and my song is Yah, / and he has become my rescue." Isaiah adds YHWH after Yah, "Yah, the LORD" (as again in 26:4); the KJV renders the pair "the LORD JEHOVAH". Zimrat may mean "song" or, from a related root, "protection, might", which fits beside "strength"; the Greek has "my praise". The Great Isaiah Scroll writes "God" twice at the start of the verse, a copying slip, but keeps "Yah, the LORD".
orig: כי עזי וזמרת יה יהוה (ki 'ozzi vezimrat Yah YHWH)

a: God is my rescue
t: Yeshu'ah, the word in Isaiah's name
p: Yeshu'ah, "salvation, rescue", appears three times in two verses. It is the root of Isaiah's name and of Jesus'.
b: Isaiah's name, Yesha'yahu, means "the LORD saves"; Joshua and Jesus (Yehoshua', Yeshua') share the root, and Matthew explains the name Jesus, "he is the one who will save his people" (Matthew 1:21). Here yeshu'ah is rendered "rescue", as in Exodus 15:2 and Psalm 118:14 on this site, which 12:2 quotes; in many places it is "salvation". The song ends the Immanuel chapters with the meaning of the prophet's own name.

a: You will draw water with joy
t: The water-drawing at the Feast of Booths
p: At the Feast of Booths, priests drew water from Siloam for the altar. Jesus' words in John 7 answer the rite.
b: The Mishnah describes the water libation at the Feast of Booths: a priest filled a golden pitcher at the pool of Siloam and poured it on the altar, and the nights were lit for dancing; "whoever has not seen the joy of the place of water-drawing has never seen joy in his life" (Mishnah Sukkah 4:9–5:1). The celebration's name, "the joy of the water-drawing", echoes this verse. On the last day of that feast Jesus cried out, "If anyone is thirsty, he should come to me and drink" (John 7:37–38). In Jewish practice 12:2–3 opens the Havdalah blessing at the end of the Sabbath, and 12:3 is the song of the Israeli folk dance Mayim Mayim.

a: Give thanks to the LORD; call out his name.
p: The first two lines match Psalm 105:1 and 1 Chronicles 16:8 word for word in Hebrew.
b: "Give thanks to the LORD; call out his name. / Let the peoples know his deeds" (Psalm 105:1; 1 Chronicles 16:8, sung when David brought the ark to Jerusalem). Isaiah's song sends Israel's praise out to "the peoples" and "all the earth" (12:5), as the flag of 11:10 had drawn the nations in. Thanksgiving here is public witness.

a: for he has acted in triumph
p: Ge'ut is from the root of Exodus 15:1, "he has risen up high, so high".
b: Ge'ut 'asah, "he has done majesty", echoes the opening of the Song of the Sea, ga'oh ga'ah, "he has risen up high, so high" (Exodus 15:1). The written text (Ketiv) reads meyudda'at, "this is known", and the read text (Qere) mudda'at, "this is being made known"; the Plain follows the Qere.

a: you who dwell in Zion
p: The Hebrew is feminine singular: Zion's people are addressed as one woman, as in "Daughter Zion".
b: Yoshevet Tsiyyon is "(woman) inhabitant of Zion", a way of addressing the city's whole population as a woman, like "Daughter Zion" (1:8; 10:32). The Great Isaiah Scroll adds "daughter": "Daughter, inhabitant of Zion". The song ends with Isaiah's title for God, "the Holy One of Israel", now not a threat (5:24) but the cause of joy, present "among you" (Zephaniah 3:14–17; Zechariah 2:10). It is a fitting end to chapters that began with "God is with us" (7:14).
